result.text: ChronoR addresses temporal link prediction on temporal knowledge graphs, a challenging problem due to non-stationary, heterogeneous data and complex temporal dependencies. Its key insight is to model relation- and time-conditioned interactions as k-dimensional rotations so that applying a learned rotation to a head-entity embedding moves it close to the corresponding tail embedding, thereby naturally encoding temporal and multi-relational dynamics. The method jointly learns dense embeddings for entities, relations, and time and parameterizes a rotation operator in high-dimensional space for each (relation, time) pair; training minimizes distance between rotated heads and tails so the model captures rich temporal–relational interactions and outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods on benchmark temporal KG link prediction tasks.

The paper tackles efficient, symmetry-preserving prediction of quantum Hamiltonian matrices for molecular systems, where maintaining SE(3) equivariance typically conflicts with computational and memory efficiency. The key insight is an architectural design that enforces SE(3)-equivariance while drastically reducing costly tensor-product operations and preventing exponential channel growth as atom types increase. The authors propose QHNet, an SE(3)-equivariant graph neural network that restructures equivariant message passing to cut tensor products by 92%, streamlines channels to limit dimensional blowup, and uses this lightweight equivariant circuitry to predict Hamiltonian entries. On four MD17 molecular datasets QHNet matches state-of-the-art accuracy with much faster runtimes and about 50% lower memory consumption.

The paper tackles the problem of choosing layerwise sparsity for magnitude-based neural network pruning, where prior work relies on heuristics or costly hyperparameter searches and performance depends critically on per-layer sparsity allocation. Their key insight is that pruning decisions should account for each layer’s contribution to the model-level ℓ2 distortion, so weight magnitudes can be rescaled into an importance score that reflects the global impact of removing parameters. They propose LAMP (layer-adaptive magnitude-based pruning), a simple, hyperparameter-free scoring scheme that rescales magnitudes by layer-level statistics to produce layerwise sparsities for global pruning, and show empirically on image classification tasks (including weight-rewinding setups) that LAMP consistently outperforms popular baselines. The method is lightweight to compute and requires no expensive tuning while yielding better sparsity–performance tradeoffs than existing layerwise allocation strategies.

The paper addresses the challenge of designing practical, high-performing active learning algorithms that work with deep neural networks by revisiting Fisher-information–based selection objectives. Its key insight is that bounds on maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) error expressed via the Fisher information can guide selection of informative batches, and that this classic criterion can be made tractable and efficient for neural models by exploiting linear-algebraic structure. The authors propose BAIT, an algorithm that selects batches by optimizing a Fisher-information–based bound on MLE error and implements this optimization with scalable matrix computations suited to modern hardware. Empirically, BAIT consistently outperforms prior active learning methods on both classification and regression tasks and is adaptable to different model architectures.

The paper tackles the problem of making neural architecture search (NAS) fast and broadly applicable to diverse, under-explored domains beyond computer vision, where AutoML could have the most impact. The key insight is that fixing a standard CNN topology but searching only over operation choices—specifically kernel sizes and dilations—gives rich multi-resolution feature extraction while dramatically reducing the search space, and that leveraging the Fourier diagonalization of convolution lets one efficiently compute mixtures of these operations. Building on this, the authors propose DASH, a differentiable NAS algorithm that uses Fourier-based diagonalization to perform weight-sharing over operation mixtures with improved asymptotic complexity, yielding up to 10× faster search in practice; they evaluate DASH on ten varied tasks (e.g., PDE solving, protein folding, heart disease detection) and show it outperforms state-of-the-art AutoML on most tasks while keeping search-plus-retraining overhead low (often under 2× the training time of a baseline CNN).

The paper addresses the slow and memory-intensive training of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) for large-scale scene reconstruction and novel view synthesis. Its key insight is that scene decomposition combined with a distributed consensus optimization—specifically using ADMM—lets multiple local 3DGS models cooperate to learn a single high-quality global model while reducing per-node load and improving convergence stability. Methodologically, DOGS splits a scene into K spatial blocks, runs K local 3DGS trainings on slave nodes that periodically enforce consensus on shared Gaussian parameters with a global model on the master via ADMM, discards the local models after training, and uses only the global model for inference; this yields over 6× faster training on large scenes while maintaining or improving rendering quality.

The paper tackles the tension in offline reinforcement learning between conservatism—necessary to avoid overestimation under distribution shift—and robustness to observation deviations (e.g., sensor noise or adversarial perturbations), which excessive conservatism can undermine. The key insight is that introducing a conservative smoothing regularizer that enforces consistency and lowered value estimates not only at dataset states but also for nearby perturbed states can simultaneously preserve safety under distribution shift and improve robustness to observation errors. Methodologically, RORL augments standard offline RL by applying regularization on both the policy and value function for states in a neighborhood around dataset states, coupled with conservative value estimation for those neighborhoods; the authors provide tighter suboptimality bounds in linear MDPs and empirically show improved benchmark performance and resilience to adversarial observation perturbations.

The paper addresses the gap between state space models (SSMs) and Transformers for language modeling by targeting efficient long-range contextualization without sacrificing short-term representational power. Its key insight is that combining an SSM sublayer—which excels at capturing long-range dependencies with subquadratic complexity—with a block-wise Transformer sublayer—which handles local, short-term interactions—yields a hybrid that leverages the strengths of both families. The authors propose the Block-State Transformer (BST), present three fully parallelizable variants that integrate SSMs and block attention, and empirically show BST outperforms comparable Transformer architectures on language modeling perplexity, generalizes to longer sequences, and achieves over an order-of-magnitude layer-level speedup versus block-recurrent baselines under model parallelism.

The paper addresses communication bottlenecks in distributed/federated optimization by unifying two previously separate approaches for gradient compression—variance-reduced unbiased compressors (DIANA) and error-feedback for biased contractive compressors (EF21)—into a single framework that can handle both. The key insight is that compressors can be characterized by two parameters (bias and variance), and by designing an algorithm that exploits both error feedback and variance-reduction ideas one can recover DIANA and EF21 as special cases while enabling a broader class of compressors. The proposed method introduces a new algorithm (EF-BV) that operates with this generalized compressor class, combines independent randomness across workers with an error-correction mechanism, and leverages variance reduction to improve convergence as the number of workers grows. The authors prove linear convergence under suitable conditions, showing that EF-BV inherits the practical benefits of biased compressors like top-k and the theoretical scaling advantages of randomized unbiased schemes.

The paper tackles catastrophic overfitting in single-step adversarial training, a sudden collapse where models become vulnerable to multi-step attacks (PGD) despite appearing robust to single-step attacks (FGSM). The key insight is that using only maximal-perturbation single-step examples concentrates training on boundary points and ignores the continuum of adversarial directions, which distorts the decision boundary and creates a highly curved loss surface that single-step updates cannot reliably defend. The authors analyze this mechanism and propose a simple remedy—augmenting or modifying single-step training to include non-maximal or diversified adversarial examples (thereby sampling the adversarial direction more broadly) to regularize curvature and preserve robustness—showing this prevents catastrophic overfitting and enables single-step procedures to resist multi-step attacks.

result.text: The paper addresses communication bottlenecks in distributed/federated optimization by unifying two previously separate approaches for gradient compression—variance-reduced unbiased compressors (DIANA) and error-feedback for biased contractive compressors (EF21)—into a single framework that can handle both. The key insight is that compressors can be characterized by two parameters (bias and variance), and by designing an algorithm that exploits both error feedback and variance-reduction ideas one can recover DIANA and EF21 as special cases while enabling a broader class of compressors. The proposed method introduces a new algorithm (EF-BV) that operates with this generalized compressor class, combines independent randomness across workers with an error-correction mechanism, and leverages variance reduction to improve convergence as the number of workers grows. The authors prove linear convergence under suitable conditions, showing that EF-BV inherits the practical benefits of biased compressors like top-k and the theoretical scaling advantages of randomized unbiased schemes.

result.text: The paper studies why fast single-step adversarial training with FGSM can suddenly fail—“catastrophic overfitting”—losing robustness during training, and questions whether the commonly used random initialization fixes the issue. The key insight is that randomness only helps by shrinking effective perturbation size and that catastrophic overfitting arises from local nonlinearity (even in tiny networks or a single filter) which makes the FGSM linear approximation invalid. To address this, the authors introduce GradAlign, a regularizer that maximizes alignment of input gradients within the perturbation set so the FGSM perturbation better matches multi-step solutions, thereby preventing overfitting and enabling effective fast adversarial training for larger ℓ∞ radii. Experiments show GradAlign narrows the robustness gap to multi-step methods while keeping training efficient.

result.text: The paper tackles the scalability bottleneck of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) training, which is typically restricted to a single GPU and thus cannot handle high-resolution or large-scale scenes; the key insight is that because each Gaussian only contributes to a small, dynamic subset of pixels, training can be distributed by communicating only the required Gaussians to the corresponding pixel partitions and dynamically balancing load. They implement this idea in Grendel, a distributed system that partitions 3DGS parameters across GPUs, uses sparse all-to-all communication to transfer relevant Gaussians to pixel shards, supports batched multi-view training (rather than one view at a time), and applies a simple sqrt(batch size) hyperparameter scaling rule. By enabling dynamic partitioning and sparse communication, Grendel scales 3DGS to tens of millions of Gaussians across many GPUs and demonstrably improves reconstruction quality on large, high-resolution scenes (e.g., raising PSNR from 26.28 to 27.28 on Rubble by moving from 11.2M Gaussians on one GPU to 40.4M on 16 GPUs).

The method, GaussianPro, iteratively propagates Gaussians by identifying reliable geometry, performing patch-based correspondences across views, and spawning new Gaussians with informed positions and normals, then optimizing the expanded set for rendering. Experiments on both large- and small-scale scenes, notably the Waymo dataset, demonstrate substantially improved reconstruction and a 1.15 dB PSNR gain over baseline 3DGS.

result.text: The paper addresses the relationship between Transformers and structured state-space models (SSMs), motivated by recent empirical results showing SSMs can rival Transformers for language modeling and the need for more efficient architectures. Its key insight is that Transformers, various attention mechanisms, and SSMs can be unified through decompositions of structured semiseparable matrices, revealing a state-space duality (SSD) that exposes equivalent computational primitives across these model families. Leveraging SSD, the authors derive generalized models and efficient algorithms that blend selective SSM behavior with attention-like operations, and they instantiate this as Mamba-2: a refinement of the Mamba selective SSM that implements the dual formulations to achieve 2–8× speedups while retaining competitive language-modeling performance.

The paper tackles the problem of reducing communication in distributed stochastic gradient methods while retaining fast convergence when using general (possibly biased) gradient compressors, where naive compression creates persistent errors that slow or break convergence and it was unknown whether error compensation can be combined with Nesterov-style acceleration. The key insight is that error compensation can be incorporated into an accelerated variance-reduced framework in a way that controls the compression error and preserves accelerated linear rates under standard smoothness and strong-convexity assumptions. Concretely, the authors design an error-compensated loopless Katyusha algorithm that maintains and corrects compression residuals while applying the loopless accelerated variance-reduction updates, and they prove an accelerated linear convergence bound for any compressor satisfying a contraction property. Empirically, the method achieves the same optimization accuracy with substantially fewer communication rounds than prior error-compensated algorithms, demonstrating that acceleration and error feedback are compatible in practice.

result.text: TempoQR addresses the problem of answering complex natural-language questions that require temporal reasoning over Temporal Knowledge Graphs (TKGs), going beyond prior work that targets only single-fact temporal queries. The key insight is that grounding a question in both entity and time-aware embedding spaces—by augmenting textual question representations with context-sensitive entity embeddings and question-specific time embeddings—enables richer temporal scope resolution and multi-hop reasoning. Methodologically, TempoQR uses three specialized modules to produce a textual question encoding, to fuse that encoding with embeddings of entities mentioned in the question, and to generate time embeddings tailored to the question’s temporal scope, then employs a transformer-based encoder to fuse these signals and predict answers from the TKG. Experiments show this embedding-based fusion approach substantially improves accuracy (by 25–45 percentage points) on complex temporal questions and generalizes better to unseen question types.

result.text: ComENet addresses the challenge of learning fully informative yet computationally efficient representations for 3D molecular graphs, where prior approaches either omit parts of 3D geometry or incur high cost. The key insight is that complete 3D information for a graph can be recovered using only carefully chosen measurements within each node’s 1-hop neighborhood—achieving both global and local completeness—by including specific rotation angles as essential coordinates and combining them with quantum-inspired basis functions. The method implements a novel 1-hop message-passing scheme that analytically encodes these angles and basis function features to guarantee completeness, provides proofs and time-complexity analysis showing orders-of-magnitude speedups over prior complete methods, and is instantiated as ComENet, which empirically delivers strong accuracy and scalability on large molecular datasets.

Methodologically, the authors derive a constant-memory procedure to compute the unrolled SGD gradient, integrate a soft-label scheme for per-class synthetic images, and apply this at scale to distill ImageNet-1K up to 50 images per class on a single GPU. result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of offline reinforcement learning where standard off-policy methods overestimate action values due to distributional shift between a static dataset and the learned policy, causing poor performance especially on complex, multi-modal data. The key insight is to learn a conservative Q-function that intentionally underestimates values for out-of-distribution actions so that the Q-estimate lower-bounds the true policy value, preventing spurious optimistic updates. Methodologically, Conservative Q-Learning (CQL) adds a simple Q-value regularizer to the Bellman error objective that penalizes Q-values of actions sampled from a broad set (e.g., policy and dataset actions) while preserving accuracy on dataset actions; this regularizer can be implemented on top of existing deep Q-learning or actor-critic algorithms and is shown theoretically to produce a value lower bound and empirically to yield substantially better returns across discrete and continuous benchmarks.

result.text: The paper addresses why state space models (SSMs), despite favorable theoretical scaling, lag behind attention-based Transformers in language modeling both in expressivity and hardware efficiency. The key insight is that existing SSMs fail mainly at recalling distant tokens and comparing tokens across a sequence—capabilities central to language modeling—and that a specialized SSM layer plus better implementation can close both the quality and speed gaps. To that end the authors introduce H3, an SSM layer explicitly designed for recall and cross-token comparison which matches attention on synthetic tasks and nearly matches or surpasses Transformers on real language benchmarks when used in hybrid models; and they introduce FlashConv, a fused-block FFT and state-passing implementation that greatly improves runtime and long-sequence scaling, enabling faster generation and competitive or superior perplexity and few-shot performance at up to multi-billion parameter scales.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of stabilizing and accelerating distributed training under contractive communication compression (e.g., Top-k) where the popular error feedback (EF) heuristic lacks satisfactory theory or practical performance without strong or impractical assumptions. Its key insight is a redesigned error-feedback mechanism (EF21) that corrects the deficiencies of prior analyses by using a different compressor-correction scheme that can be analyzed under standard assumptions in the heterogeneous-data distributed setting, yielding provably faster rates without resorting to unbiased compressors or bounded-gradient hypotheses. Methodologically, the authors propose the EF21 algorithm which modifies how compression errors are accumulated and compensated across workers, prove an O(1/T) convergence rate for smooth nonconvex objectives (improving over the previous O(1/T^{2/3}) guarantee) and show linear convergence under the PL condition, and validate that EF21 consistently outperforms classical EF in experiments.

result.text: The paper addresses few-shot temporal knowledge graph reasoning: predicting future facts for newly emerging entities in evolving temporal knowledge graphs where only very limited historical observations exist and distributions may shift over time. The key insight is that rigid, one-size-fits-all neighbor sampling and aggregation fails under both data scarcity and temporal drift, so the model should learn to dynamically adapt how it selects and pools recent contextual facts for each new entity using feedback from future facts. To do this the authors propose MetaTKGR, a meta-learning framework that jointly learns temporally supervised sampling and aggregation strategies and a temporal adaptation regularizer to stabilize updates, enabling rapid, time-aware adaptation for new entities; theory and experiments on three real-world TKGs show substantial gains over static and prior meta-learning baselines.

result.text: The paper addresses how to theoretically ground and improve soft threshold pruning, a top-performing neural network pruning approach whose prior threshold-tuning strategies lacked unified explanation. The key insight is that soft threshold pruning can be reformulated as solving an implicit L1-regularized optimization problem via the Iterative Shrinkage-Thresholding Algorithm (ISTA), which reveals that different empirical threshold schedulers correspond to different ways of tuning the L1 penalty and that maintaining a stable L1 coefficient yields a time-invariant objective. Building on this view, the authors derive an optimal threshold scheduler and a family of pruning methods—including sparsify-during-training, early pruning, and pruning-at-initialization—that keep the regularization coefficient stable, and they validate the approach with state-of-the-art results on ResNet-50, MobileNet-V1 and SEW ResNet-18 on ImageNet.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of selecting a small, informative subset of training data (data pruning) when labels are noisy and training uses re-labeling methods that correct annotation errors; existing pruning approaches don’t account for which subset best enables accurate re-labeling across the whole dataset. The key insight is that an example’s chance of being correctly re-labeled depends on the prediction confidence of its neighbors within the chosen subset, so maximizing aggregate neighborhood confidence will maximize re-labeling accuracy and downstream generalization. Based on this, the authors propose Prune4Rel, an algorithm that selects a subset by optimizing total neighborhood prediction confidence for all training examples, thereby encouraging reliable local consensus for re-labeling; experiments on multiple noisy and synthetic datasets show substantial gains over baselines with both re-labeling and standard training.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of reinforcement learning in environments with extremely sparse rewards, where naïve exploration rarely yields informative feedback and existing algorithms struggle to learn in reasonable time. Its key insight is that sub-optimal offline demonstrations can be used as guidance (not imitation) to orient online policy improvement toward promising parts of the state-action space while still permitting learning beyond the demonstrator’s performance. The proposed LOGO algorithm interleaves standard policy improvement with a guidance step that leverages offline demonstration data to bias exploration and value updates, includes a theoretical lower bound on per-episode improvement, and is extended to handle censored (partial) observations in the demonstrations. Empirically, LOGO outperforms prior methods on sparse-reward benchmarks and on a mobile-robot trajectory-tracking and obstacle-avoidance task.

result.text: The paper addresses limitations of standard sequence models—RNNs’ training instability and limited, sequential memory and CNNs’ fixed, discrete receptive fields that prevent handling arbitrarily long or irregularly sampled sequences. Its key insight is to parameterize convolutional kernels as continuous functions rather than fixed discrete filters, enabling a single convolution operation to evaluate the kernel at any set of input positions and thus model arbitrarily long, non-uniformly sampled, or irregular sequences in parallel. The method implements Continuous Kernel Convolution (CKConv) by learning small neural networks (continuous kernel generators) that map relative positions to kernel values, and builds CKCNNs by replacing traditional discrete kernels with these continuous kernels to compute convolutions over arbitrary locations; this yields state-of-the-art performance on benchmarks like permuted MNIST and handles irregular sampling faster and simpler than neural ODE approaches.

result.text: The paper addresses limitations in knowledge graph link prediction where typical embedding-based models combine entity and relation vectors with simple additive or concatenation-based interactions, which cannot express relation-specific projections of source entities. The key insight is to treat relations as context that generates the parameters of the function applied to source-entity embeddings, enabling richer, relation-conditioned transformations instead of fixed, shared matrices. Concretely, the authors use relation embeddings to parameterize (generate) parts of the scoring model applied to entity embeddings and integrate this contextual parameter generation into two existing link-prediction architectures—including the prior state-of-the-art—thereby increasing representational capacity. This approach yields significant accuracy improvements, sets a new state-of-the-art on benchmarks, and speeds convergence by up to 28×.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of predicting event times in temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs), where embedding-based ranking approaches struggle to capture temporal order and distance relationships and to provide interpretable, robust predictions under limited or imbalanced data. The key insight is to convert a TKG into a temporal event knowledge graph (TEKG) that explicitly represents time as nodes, enabling logical reasoning over temporal structure and the use of probabilistic rules tied to query intervals. The method implements a differentiable random walk on the TEKG to aggregate evidence from temporal and relational paths, and associates logical rules with conditional probability density functions over intervals to produce interval-based time predictions and explanations. Empirically, TEILP outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across five benchmarks and shows improved robustness in low-data, imbalanced, and forecasting-only scenarios while offering interpretable rule-based justifications.

result.text: The paper tackles offline reinforcement learning, where the challenge is to learn reliable policies from fixed logged data without environment interaction, focusing on avoiding overoptimistic behavior in regions poorly covered by the dataset. Its key insight is to cast model-based offline RL as a two-player zero-sum game in which an adversarial dynamics model is trained to both fit the dataset and minimize the policy’s estimated value, thereby inducing pessimism where the data is scarce. The method, RAMBO, alternates between policy optimization inside the learned model and adversarial model updates that trade off data likelihood with value minimization, yielding a conservative value estimate that provably lower-bounds true performance under PAC-style guarantees. Empirically, RAMBO achieves stronger and more robust performance than prior state-of-the-art offline RL baselines on standard benchmarks.

result.text: The paper addresses improving transfer-based adversarial attacks—crafting examples on a surrogate model that reliably fool other unseen models—by targeting regions of the loss landscape that yield examples with better cross-model generalization. The key insight is that adversarial examples located in flat local maxima (low curvature regions) transfer better, so they augment the attack objective with a gradient-norm penalty to favor flatness. Because directly computing Hessian-based curvature is costly, they approximate the regularizer with a first-order approximation that interpolates neighboring gradients via random sample-based finite differences and reduce variance by averaging gradients over multiple random samples during iterative updates. Experiments on an ImageNet-compatible benchmark show the method produces flatter adversarial regions and substantially improves transferability against both normally and adversarially trained models compared to prior attacks.

result.text: The paper tackles the question of which unlabeled examples to query in active learning by directly linking selection to downstream test performance: it proves that choosing unlabeled samples with larger gradient norms yields a tighter upper bound on test loss and thus better generalization. The key insight is that gradient norm of an example—reflecting how much it would change model parameters if labeled—predicts its value for reducing test error, but since true gradients require labels, the authors approximate them using two schemes. They propose expected-gradnorm, which estimates gradient norm via an expected empirical loss over label distributions, and entropy-gradnorm, which uses an unsupervised entropy-based surrogate, and combine both into a unified active learning framework that outperforms prior methods on image classification, semantic segmentation, and noisy cellular imaging tasks.

The paper addresses whether convolutional neural networks can regain competitiveness with transformers by scaling convolutional kernels far beyond the common 31x31 limit without incurring performance saturation or prohibitive costs. The key insight is that sparsity and factorization can be used to compose extremely large receptive fields efficiently: by representing large kernels as sparse, factorized blocks (mixing dense center regions with sparse outer rings and channel-wise factorization) one can maintain expressivity while controlling parameter and compute growth. Methodologically, the authors develop a recipe for sparse large kernels and implement it in a pure-CNN architecture called Sparse Large Kernel Network (SLaK), which uses sparse factorized 51x51 (and up to 61x61) convolutions within a hierarchical backbone and demonstrate parity or improvements over state-of-the-art transformers and modern ConvNets across ImageNet classification and downstream detection/segmentation benchmarks.

result.text: The paper addresses reducing uplink communication in federated learning under realistic challenges—partial client participation and heterogeneous data—while handling the distortion introduced by communication compression. Its key insight is that the classical stochastic controlled averaging (SCA) can be reformulated into an equivalent but simpler and more communication-efficient implementation that halves uplink cost and serves as a foundation for compression-aware algorithms. Building on that reformulation, the authors develop two algorithms—SCALLION for unbiased compressors and SCAFCOM for biased compressors—that integrate compressed updates without extra assumptions on compression error or limits on heterogeneity, and they prove improved communication and computation complexity relative to prior work. Empirically, both methods match full-precision FL performance with much less uplink transmission and beat recent compressed-FL baselines under the same communication budget.

result.text: The paper addresses understanding how the curvature of the loss landscape, as captured by the Hessian eigenspectrum, varies across layers of deep neural networks and how that can inform regularization to improve generalization. The key insight is that layerwise Hessian geometry closely mirrors the full-network Hessian, with middle layers’ eigenspectra most similar to the overall spectrum, and that both the maximum eigenvalue and the Hessian trace decrease during training. The authors analyze per-layer Hessian eigenspectra empirically across architectures and datasets and propose a regularizer that penalizes the trace of the Hessian at each layer (or selectively at middle layers), which steers SGD toward flatter minima and yields improved generalization in experiments.

result.text: The paper addresses the limitation of neural network-based wave functions that can only model different geometries of the same fixed set of atoms, preventing a single model from generalizing across molecules with different compositions. The key insight is to learn transferable local electronic representations via graph-based message passing that connect molecular orbitals to covalent bonds, enabling embeddings that capture local electronic structure common to multiple molecules. The authors introduce Globe, a graph-learned orbital embedding scheme, and Moon, a size-consistent molecular orbital network Ansatz that uses those embeddings to jointly solve Schrödinger equations for different molecules; empirically Moon converges about 4.5× faster to comparable or lower energies and yields additive energy scaling with system size where prior methods diverged. Together, Globe and Moon demonstrate for the first time that a single neural wave function can generalize across molecules with different atoms.

result.text: The paper tackles hardware-aware structural pruning: how to remove filters from neural networks to maximize accuracy while meeting a device-specific latency budget. The key insight is to combine a fast-to-evaluate global saliency score (estimating accuracy loss) with a latency lookup table (estimating per-filter latency reduction) and cast pruning as a reward-maximization resource allocation problem. Methodologically, they reformulate global structural pruning as a constrained knapsack-like optimization and solve it with an augmented knapsack solver that selects filters to drop based on joint latency and saliency rewards, yielding efficient pruning that outperforms prior methods across classification and detection benchmarks and multiple target platforms.

result.text: The paper addresses robustness of reinforcement learning when an adversary perturbs state observations, a realistic threat model for adversarial attacks and noisy sensing in deployed agents. The key insight is that for a fixed agent policy one can compute (and therefore learn) an optimal adversary that provably minimizes the agent’s return, and that alternatingly training the agent against such a learned adversary produces stronger robustness than prior heuristic attacks. Concretely, the authors propose an Alternating Training with Learned Adversaries (ATLA) framework that jointly and online trains a policy-gradient adversary alongside the agent following the optimal-adversary formulation, and they show both theoretically and empirically—including improvements from using history-aware (LSTM) policies inspired by SA-MDP analysis—that ATLA yields state-of-the-art robustness on continuous control benchmarks.

result.text: The paper addresses communication bottlenecks in distributed/federated optimization by unifying two previously separate approaches for gradient compression—variance-reduced unbiased compressors (DIANA) and error-feedback for biased contractive compressors (EF21)—into a single framework that can handle both. The key insight is that compressors can be characterized by two parameters (bias and variance), and by designing an algorithm that exploits both error feedback and variance-reduction ideas one can recover DIANA and EF21 as special cases while enabling a broader class of compressors. The proposed method introduces a new algorithm (EF-BV) that operates with this generalized compressor class, combines independent randomness across workers with an error-correction mechanism, and leverages variance reduction to improve convergence as the number of workers grows. The authors prove linear convergence under suitable conditions, showing that EF-BV inherits the practical benefits of biased compressors like top-k and the theoretical scaling advantages of randomized unbiased schemes.

result.text: The paper addresses overfitting in deep neural networks by proposing a lightweight regularization technique that improves generalization, robustness, and performance across tasks. The key insight is to randomly sample subnet widths and apply transformed training samples so that these sub-networks receive self-guided perturbations to their raw gradients—termed Gradient Augmentation (GradAug)—which encourages diverse, well-generalized representations. Methodologically, during training the model samples different widths of the original network and feeds randomly transformed inputs to regularize those sub-networks, injecting gradient-level disturbances without architectural change; this simple procedure is compatible with various models and tasks and yields strong empirical gains (e.g., ResNet-50 to 78.79% on ImageNet, 79.67% with CutMix) while improving robustness and low-data performance.

The paper tackles temporal knowledge graph completion (TKGC), the problem of predicting missing time-stamped facts in a knowledge graph by leveraging learned latent representations of entities, relations, and times. Its key insight is that box embeddings—regions in embedding space that naturally model set inclusion, overlap, and relational asymmetry—can be extended to the temporal setting to capture complex time-varying relational patterns while maintaining full expressiveness and strong inductive capacity. The proposed model, BoxTE, adapts the static BoxE architecture by incorporating timestamp-specific transformations and boxes that represent when facts hold, training these embeddings to score triples with timestamps so that correct temporal facts lie in appropriate boxes; theoretical analysis proves expressiveness and empirical evaluation across benchmarks shows state-of-the-art performance.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of building graph neural networks that are equivariant to Euclidean transformations (rotations, translations, reflections) and node permutations—crucial for physical and geometric tasks—without the computational burden of high-order representations and with scalability beyond 3D. The key insight is that equivariance can be maintained by designing message-passing updates that couple scalar node features and pairwise relative positional vectors through simple, learnable functions that act only on invariant scalars and produce equivariant vector outputs, avoiding costly tensor-valued intermediate features. The proposed E(n)-Equivariant Graph Neural Network (EGNN) uses edge-wise functions of relative distances and node features to update positions and features in an equivariant manner, enabling efficient, scalable message passing applicable to arbitrary dimensional Euclidean spaces. Empirically, EGNNs achieve competitive or superior performance on tasks including dynamical system prediction, graph autoencoder representation learning, and molecular property prediction while remaining computationally lightweight.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of finding compact, high-performing sparse neural networks without the costly multi-stage pipeline of traditional pruning methods. Its key insight is to jointly learn both network weights and a trainable, layer-wise pruning threshold via backpropagation so that the sparse structure is adapted dynamically during standard training rather than imposed afterward. The method introduces masked layers with learnable thresholds that push small-magnitude activations/weights to zero and are optimized alongside weights, enabling the model to reach high sparsity with little performance loss in the same number of epochs as dense training. Empirical results show competitive or superior sparsity–accuracy tradeoffs across architectures and reveal that dynamic, fine-grained thresholding exposes limitations of three-stage pruning and offers guidance for designing inherently compact networks.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of designing practical, high-performing active learning algorithms that work with deep neural networks by revisiting Fisher-information–based selection objectives. Its key insight is that bounds on maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) error expressed via the Fisher information can guide selection of informative batches, and that this classic criterion can be made tractable and efficient for neural models by exploiting linear-algebraic structure. The authors propose BAIT, an algorithm that selects batches by optimizing a Fisher-information–based bound on MLE error and implements this optimization with scalable matrix computations suited to modern hardware. Empirically, BAIT consistently outperforms prior active learning methods on both classification and regression tasks and is adaptable to different model architectures.

The paper addresses the problem of selecting convolutional kernel sizes in CNNs—a hyperparameter that ideally should vary across layers and data but is expensive to search and poorly served by prior learnable-size approaches that use dilation and have limited descriptive bandwidth. The key insight is that one can learn continuous, high-bandwidth convolution kernels whose effective size is differentiable and adjustable during training without increasing parameter count, and that controlling kernel frequency content analytically avoids aliasing when scaling to larger effective receptive fields or higher-resolution inputs. The method, called FlexConv, parameterizes kernels in a continuous differentiable form (with a novel frequency-controllable parameterization) that lets the network learn kernel size and spectral properties end-to-end, enabling FlexNets that model long-range dependencies without pooling, generalize to larger resolutions, converge faster, and achieve strong performance on sequential and image benchmarks while outperforming prior learned-size and dilated-kernel approaches.

args.text: We propose Distill4Fast-AT: a robust dataset distillation objective that bakes in curvature control and gradient-alignment priors so that models trained with cheap, single-step adversarial training on the distilled set achieve PGD-level robustness on real data. Concretely, the bilevel objective optimizes synthetic images/labels so that a student trained only with diversified, non-maximal single-step adversaries on the distilled data attains strong robustness on a held-out real set, while (i) penalizing Hessian-trace proxies around synthetic samples to enforce flatness and (ii) adding a GradAlign-style term to align FGSM and multi-step gradients within the ε-ball. During the inner student updates on synthetic data, we use a FOSC-based schedule to gradually tighten attack convergence, ensuring early efficiency and late-stage high-quality adversaries without incurring full PGD cost throughout. This combination is designed to prevent catastrophic overfitting in fast-AT, transferring the distilled flatness/alignment priors to downstream training and yielding strong robustness at substantially reduced compute.

args.text: I propose Dual-Controlled ISTA Pruning (DIP), a training-time, hardware-aware pruning scheme that couples soft-threshold (ISTA-style) sparsification with a dual ascent controller to meet a target speedup exactly. We insert learnable, per-layer soft-threshold masks and optimize a constrained objective: minimize task loss plus layerwise L1 penalties while enforcing a differentiable latency surrogate built from a per-layer LUT; per-layer L1 coefficients (or thresholds) are updated by projected dual steps based on the current latency gap, automatically reallocating sparsity to the layers with best accuracy-per-speed benefit. This unifies threshold-learning during training with hardware-constrained allocation and extends to structured/N:M patterns by grouping proximal updates and using pattern-specific LUTs. Compared to post-hoc DP/knapsack allocators, DIP delivers one-shot training that directly targets latency budgets and preserves accuracy by continuously steering sparsity where it hurts least.

Methodologically, the authors instantiate this framework to derive convergence rates for a family of 16 new methods, including EC-SGD-DIANA (error feedback plus biased compression of gradient differences) and EC-LSVRG-DIANA (adding variance reduction for finite-sum problems), and prove these methods converge to the exact optimum in expectation with a constant stepsize for convex and strongly convex objectives when workers compute full or variance-reduced gradients.

result.text: The paper tackles catastrophic overfitting in single-step adversarial training, a sudden collapse where models become vulnerable to multi-step attacks (PGD) despite appearing robust to single-step attacks (FGSM). The key insight is that using only maximal-perturbation single-step examples concentrates training on boundary points and ignores the continuum of adversarial directions, which distorts the decision boundary and creates a highly curved loss surface that single-step updates cannot reliably defend. The authors analyze this mechanism and propose a simple remedy—augmenting or modifying single-step training to include non-maximal or diversified adversarial examples (thereby sampling the adversarial direction more broadly) to regularize curvature and preserve robustness—showing this prevents catastrophic overfitting and enables single-step procedures to resist multi-step attacks.

result.text: The paper addresses temporal knowledge graph event forecasting, specifically the difficulty of predicting future interactions for entities lacking useful historical recurrence or periodicity. Its key insight is that future events arise from both historical dependencies and unobserved non-historical factors, so modeling and contrasting these two sources can reveal whether a query depends on past events and which candidate entities are most plausible. The proposed Contrastive Event Network (CENET) learns historical and non-historical dependency signals, uses contrastive learning on query representations to decide whether the current moment is history-driven, trains a binary classifier to produce a boolean mask over candidate entities, and applies this mask during inference to improve ranking. Evaluated on five benchmarks, CENET substantially outperforms prior methods, notably improving Hits@1 by at least 8.3% on event-based datasets.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of learning from eigenvector-based spectral representations on graphs and meshes while correctly handling the intrinsic symmetries of eigenvectors—namely sign flips and arbitrary orthonormal basis choices within degenerate eigenspaces—which otherwise break downstream learning and limit expressiveness. The key insight is to build architectures that are provably invariant to these symmetries, so any function learned from eigenvectors respects sign- and basis-equivalence and thus depends only on the intrinsic spectral information. The authors propose two neural architectures, SignNet for sign-flip invariance and BasisNet for full basis invariance, prove universal approximation results showing these networks can represent any continuous invariant function of eigenvectors, and show that when applied to Laplacian eigenvectors they strictly generalize existing spectral graph convolutions, positional encodings, and other spectral invariants. Empirically, SignNet and BasisNet outperform prior spectral baselines on tasks including molecular graph regression, expressive graph representation learning, and neural fields on triangle meshes.

result.text: The paper addresses one-shot/post-training compression of deep neural networks, where an already-trained model must be pruned and/or quantized accurately using only a small calibration set and without retraining. The key insight is that the Optimal Brain Surgeon (OBS) framework—originally designed for pruning by using second-order (Hessian) information to assess parameter importance—can be efficiently and exactly realized at modern DNN scale and extended to handle weight quantization as well, enabling principled joint treatment of pruning and quantization. Methodologically, the authors derive scalable algorithms to compute and apply OBS-style second-order updates for both removing and discretizing weights, optimizing a local quadratic approximation of the loss to minimize accuracy loss under compression while remaining time- and space-efficient. Empirically, this unified OBS-based approach yields substantially better post-training compression–accuracy trade-offs than prior methods and enables accurate compound pruning-plus-quantization without retraining.

Its key insight is an adaptive extension of randomized smoothing theory—specifically an adaptive Neyman-Pearson lemma—that allows certification of the total cumulative reward rather than requiring the policy to be robust at every intermediate step, thereby accounting for attackers whose perturbations can depend stochastically on past observations and actions. args.text: We propose ODySSey, an online duality‑guided sparse attentive SSM that closes Mamba’s non‑standard retrieval gap without resorting to heavy attention. At each step, a tiny sparse attention probe (local+random+global anchors) selects a few salient remote tokens; using state‑space duality, we compile the effect of these edges into a rank‑k semiseparable update of the SSM transition/kernel, yielding a causal low‑rank modification to the selective SSM that preserves O(nk) time and constant‑state memory. Integrated with a sliding‑window attention for exact short‑range recall, the layer learns the probe and the compilation jointly, and at inference performs only top‑k retrieval and a fused low‑rank state update. We expect strong gains on long‑context retrieval and in‑context learning tasks where pure Mamba struggles, with throughput comparable to selective SSMs and far below full or blockwise attention.

args.text: We propose a gauge-equivariant operator network for molecular Hamiltonians that enforces both SE(3) equivariance and invariance/equivariance to local unitary changes of the atomic-orbital basis (U(d_l) per atom and angular-momentum channel). The model performs equivariant message passing to predict reduced Wigner–Eckart coefficients and reconstructs the full AO Hamiltonian via precomputed Clebsch–Gordan/Gaunt tensors, inducing block-sparse selection rules; efficiency is retained by mixing Cartesian tensors for cheap feature interactions. Training uses supervised targets from large Hamiltonian datasets together with gauge-invariant regularizers on spectra and density-matrix projectors, enforcing Hermiticity and consistency across basis reparameterizations and localized-orbital gauges. Compared to existing SE(3)-equivariant Hamiltonian predictors, this should improve data efficiency and cross-basis transfer while remaining lightweight, leveraging basis-invariant architectures and transferable orbital embeddings to generalize across molecules.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of reliably estimating the Fisher information matrix (FIM) in deep learning, where the true FIM is intractable and practitioners must use empirical estimators whose quality depends on estimator variance. The key insight is that two unbiased, consistent estimators derived from equivalent FIM representations have analytically tractable variance expressions that reveal how a network’s parameterization and data interplay determine estimation noise. The authors derive closed-form variance formulas and upper bounds, analyze how network structure (e.g., layer widths, parameter coupling) influences those variances, and interpret these results to inform when sample-based FIM estimates are trustworthy for tasks like second-order optimization and geometric analysis.

The paper addresses the problem that standard CNNs must be custom-designed for specific tasks because their discrete, local kernels and reliance on downsampling/depth make them sensitive to input resolution, length, and dimensionality. The key insight is that replacing discrete kernels with continuous convolutional kernels that model long-range dependencies at every layer lets a single architecture operate across arbitrary resolutions and spatial dimensions without structural changes. The method, called Continuous Convolutional Neural Network (CCNN), implements continuous kernels within convolutional layers to capture global context and avoid task-specific downsampling, and the authors demonstrate that the same CCNN architecture can be applied to 1D sequential, 2D image, and 3D point-cloud tasks, matching or outperforming specialized state-of-the-art models.

args.text: Large-scale 3D Gaussian Splatting suffers from synchronization bottlenecks and straggler sensitivity when distributed across heterogeneous or unreliable clusters. We propose a wait-free decentralized consensus scheme that replaces master-centric ADMM with pairwise proximal averaging over a rotating exponential-graph neighbor schedule: each worker optimizes its spatial block while maintaining boundary "ghost Gaussians" and asynchronously exchanging only deltas for Gaussians that influence remote pixels. Communication is routed sparsely, Grendel-style, to the pixel shards that need them, and consensus uses staleness-aware weights (recency and photometric residual variance) to approximate ADMM dual steps while achieving near-exact averaging as the topology mixes. This yields ADMM-like stability without global barriers, improving wall-clock convergence and rendering quality on large, high-resolution scenes and enabling robust edge/decentralized mapping.

args.text: We propose Gauge-Equivariant AO Hamiltonian Networks (GE-AOHN), which predict molecular Hamiltonians while being equivariant to both global SE(3) motions and local per-atom orbital-basis rotations within each l-shell (the intrinsic AO gauge). args.text: We propose Amortized Active Query Policies: a learnable policy that maps the current model state and a compact sketch of the unlabeled pool to a query set in a single forward pass, enabling real-time streaming decisions and million-scale batch selection. The policy is meta-trained across tasks using sequential contrastive information bounds and distilled supervision from strong but expensive teachers (e.g., Fisher-information–based and expected-gradient-norm objectives), while incorporating differentiable diversity/coverage regularizers to prevent redundancy at very large batch sizes. At deployment, the policy matches a target query rate and approximates BAIT/grad-norm quality with orders-of-magnitude lower per-decision cost, generalizing across datasets and shifts. This unifies streaming control with scalable selection and yields hardware-aware, latency-bounded active learning.

We propose Dynamic Continuous Sparse Convolution (DCSC), which unifies continuous-kernel parameterizations with learnable sparse sampling and anti-aliased scaling. A kernel is represented as a frequency-controlled continuous function, but each output is computed by evaluating it at a small, content-adaptive set of continuous offsets per location via a differentiable quadrature scheme, combining the expressivity of continuous kernels with the efficiency of learned sparse taps. The kernel’s spectral bandwidth is explicitly modulated as a function of the offsets and input resolution to enforce anti-aliasing, yielding resolution-agnostic behavior and stable generalization when scaling receptive fields. Conceptually, DCSC instantiates a learned quadrature of an integral operator with nodes and weights predicted by the network, enabling large effective receptive fields at low cost and improving over static learnable spacing on high-resolution vision and irregularly sampled sequence tasks.

result.text: The paper addresses the trade-off in decentralized learning between minimizing per-iteration communication (by contacting few neighbors) and maintaining fast network-wide information mixing, noting that common topologies either require high node degrees or mix poorly as network size grows. The key insight is that one can design sparse, communication-efficient topologies whose consensus (mixing) rate does not degrade with network size, by balancing node degrees and using time-varying neighbor selections so that information spreads rapidly despite low per-iteration connectivity. Concretely, the authors propose EquiTopo, a family including EquiStatic—an almost-regular static graph with degree Θ(log n)—and EquiDyn—a time-varying one-peer topology generated by a random sampling procedure; both achieve an n-independent consensus rate and are plugged into decentralized SGD and gradient-tracking algorithms to yield provably faster communication and improved convergence, corroborated by experiments and a BlueFog implementation.

result.text: The paper addresses molecular conformation generation—predicting stable 3D atomic coordinates from 2D molecular graphs—where prior methods first predict interatomic distances and then reconstruct coordinates, a pipeline that compounds errors from noisy distance predictions. The key insight is to bypass explicit distance-to-coordinate reconstruction by directly learning the gradient field of the log density (the score) of atomic coordinates, which lets one sample stable conformations via Langevin dynamics; to handle the roto-translation equivariance of coordinate scores, the authors show this is equivalent to estimating score fields over interatomic distances. result.text: We propose Amortized Active Query Policies: a learnable policy that maps the current model state and a compact sketch of the unlabeled pool to a query set in a single forward pass, enabling real-time streaming decisions and million-scale batch selection. The policy is meta-trained across tasks using sequential contrastive information bounds and distilled supervision from strong but expensive teachers (e.g., Fisher-information–based and expected-gradient-norm objectives), while incorporating differentiable diversity/coverage regularizers to prevent redundancy at very large batch sizes. At deployment, the policy matches a target query rate and approximates BAIT/grad-norm quality with orders-of-magnitude lower per-decision cost, generalizing across datasets and shifts. This unifies streaming control with scalable selection and yields hardware-aware, latency-bounded active learning.

result.text: We propose Dynamic Continuous Sparse Convolution (DCSC), which unifies continuous-kernel parameterizations with learnable sparse sampling and anti-aliased scaling. A kernel is represented as a frequency-controlled continuous function, but each output is computed by evaluating it at a small, content-adaptive set of continuous offsets per location via a differentiable quadrature scheme, combining the expressivity of continuous kernels with the efficiency of learned sparse taps. The kernel’s spectral bandwidth is explicitly modulated as a function of the offsets and input resolution to enforce anti-aliasing, yielding resolution-agnostic behavior and stable generalization when scaling receptive fields. Conceptually, DCSC instantiates a learned quadrature of an integral operator with nodes and weights predicted by the network, enabling large effective receptive fields at low cost and improving over static learnable spacing on high-resolution vision and irregularly sampled sequence tasks.

result.text: Large-scale 3D Gaussian Splatting suffers from synchronization bottlenecks and straggler sensitivity when distributed across heterogeneous or unreliable clusters. We propose a wait-free decentralized consensus scheme that replaces master-centric ADMM with pairwise proximal averaging over a rotating exponential-graph neighbor schedule: each worker optimizes its spatial block while maintaining boundary "ghost Gaussians" and asynchronously exchanging only deltas for Gaussians that influence remote pixels. Communication is routed sparsely, Grendel-style, to the pixel shards that need them, and consensus uses staleness-aware weights (recency and photometric residual variance) to approximate ADMM dual steps while achieving near-exact averaging as the topology mixes. This yields ADMM-like stability without global barriers, improving wall-clock convergence and rendering quality on large, high-resolution scenes and enabling robust edge/decentralized mapping.

result.text: We propose Gauge-Equivariant AO Hamiltonian Networks (GE-AOHN), which predict molecular Hamiltonians while being equivariant to both global SE(3) motions and local per-atom orbital-basis rotations within each l-shell (the intrinsic AO gauge). result.text: I propose Dual-Controlled ISTA Pruning (DIP), a training-time, hardware-aware pruning scheme that couples soft-threshold (ISTA-style) sparsification with a dual ascent controller to meet a target speedup exactly. The key insight is that communication-efficient compression can itself amplify privacy: by having each client send only a randomly selected partial sketch of its data, the effective privacy loss per client is reduced, allowing optimal privacy-accuracy trade-offs with far fewer bits than uncompressed protocols. Concretely, the authors prove that optimal error under (ε,δ)-DP can be achieved when each client transmits Θ(n·min(ε,ε^2)) bits for mean estimation and Θ(log(n·min(ε,ε^2))) bits for frequency estimation, yielding substantial savings whenever n·min(ε,ε^2)=o(d). Their method constructs randomized compression schemes and sampling-based communication protocols that integrate with noise addition to meet (ε,δ)-DP while exploiting privacy amplification from partial, randomly selected transmissions.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of designing decentralized optimization algorithms that remain stable and converge linearly when inter-node communication is compressed, a setting where prior methods suffer from slow convergence or instability due to data heterogeneity and accumulating compression error. The key insight is that the unrolled gradient used by MTT can be computed exactly with constant memory complexity, enabling a ~6x reduction in memory footprint, and that class-rich datasets benefit from a novel soft label assignment to improve convergence. Methodologically, the authors derive a constant-memory procedure to compute the unrolled SGD gradient, integrate a soft-label scheme for per-class synthetic images, and apply this at scale to distill ImageNet-1K up to 50 images per class on a single GPU. The resulting algorithm achieves new state-of-the-art distilled-data performance on ImageNet-1K—using only 4.2% of the original data with a 5.9% accuracy gap to full-data training and an 18.2% absolute gain over prior SOTA.

args.text: We propose Meta-RuleSwitch, a few-shot, explainable temporal KG forecaster that meta-learns an entity- and time-specific prior over temporal logical rules together with a copy-vs-reason gating policy to handle sparsity and drift. Concretely, we couple a differentiable temporal rule learner (temporal random walks with interval scoring) with a copy-generation head for recurring facts, and train a contrastive gate that routes queries to copying or rule-based reasoning; a meta-learning objective enables rapid adaptation of rule weights and the gate from a tiny, recent support set for emerging entities. result.text: We propose ODySSey, an online duality‑guided sparse attentive SSM that closes Mamba’s non‑standard retrieval gap without resorting to heavy attention. At each step, a tiny sparse attention probe (local+random+global anchors) selects a few salient remote tokens; using state‑space duality, we compile the effect of these edges into a rank‑k semiseparable update of the SSM transition/kernel, yielding a causal low‑rank modification to the selective SSM that preserves O(nk) time and constant‑state memory. Integrated with a sliding‑window attention for exact short‑range recall, the layer learns the probe and the compilation jointly, and at inference performs only top‑k retrieval and a fused low‑rank state update. We expect strong gains on long‑context retrieval and in‑context learning tasks where pure Mamba struggles, with throughput comparable to selective SSMs and far below full or blockwise attention.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of communication overhead in data-parallel SGD when using fixed, heuristic gradient quantization schemes that do not account for changing gradient statistics during training. The key insight is that gradient distributions evolve over time and that adapting the quantizer to these changing statistics—by estimating sufficient statistics of a simple parametric model in parallel—yields better compression without degrading optimization. The authors propose two adaptive schemes, ALQ and AMQ, in which each worker periodically computes and shares compact statistics to update its local quantizer parameters efficiently, enabling synchronized, low-cost adaptation across processors. Empirically, these methods improve validation accuracy (≈2% on CIFAR-10, ≈1% on ImageNet) in low-communication budgets and show greater robustness to hyperparameter choices.

args.text: I propose a history-gated temporal rule–embedding mixture that jointly forecasts future links and their occurrence times in temporal knowledge graphs. A TEKG random-walk rule expert produces an interpretable interval density and candidate ranking by grounding temporal logical rules, while an embedding expert (with time-aware transformations) handles novel, non-repetitive interactions and long-range drifts. A contrastive, history-vs-nonhistory gate routes queries and calibrates mixture weights, with a consistency loss tying the rule-based time density to the embedding scores (e.g., downweighting candidates implausible at high-probability times) under interval-censored supervision. This end-to-end training yields improved accuracy, temporal calibration, and interpretability under data scarcity and distribution shift.

result.text: The paper addresses the need for accurate, efficient prediction of electronic Hamiltonian matrices—fundamental quantities that determine quantum states and properties of molecules—that current quantum chemistry datasets do not provide at scale. Its key insight is that supplying high-quality Hamiltonians alongside diverse geometries enables supervised ML models to learn transferable mappings from molecular structure to Hamiltonian, allowing prediction for arbitrary molecules and accelerating downstream electronic-structure tasks. result.text: The paper addresses improving transfer-based adversarial attacks—crafting examples on a surrogate model that reliably fool other unseen models—by targeting regions of the loss landscape that yield examples with better cross-model generalization. The key insight is that adversarial examples located in flat local maxima (low curvature regions) transfer better, so they augment the attack objective with a gradient-norm penalty to favor flatness. Because directly computing Hessian-based curvature is costly, they approximate the regularizer with a first-order approximation that interpolates neighboring gradients via random sample-based finite differences and reduce variance by averaging gradients over multiple random samples during iterative updates. result.text: The paper addresses the problem of selecting node locations and weights for approximating functions in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) — a core issue in kernel interpolation, quadrature, and density estimation — with guarantees that hold broadly across kernels. The key insight is to introduce continuous volume sampling (VS), a continuous analogue of Deshpande & Vempala’s discrete volume sampling, which yields near-optimal error bounds that depend only on the spectrum of the RKHS integration operator and thus apply to any Mercer kernel. Methodologically, the authors define the VS probability density in terms of determinants of kernel matrices evaluated at continuous points, show how its pdf can be computed using only pointwise kernel evaluations (making it amenable to MCMC sampling), and prove almost-optimal interpolation and quadrature error bounds under VS without relying on leverage-score approximations or determinantal point process machinery.

args.text: I propose Second-Order Latency-Constrained Structured Sparse Training (SOLST): during training, we update group-wise pruning masks by solving an OBS-style proximal step on a local quadratic loss using cheap block-diagonal/diagonal Hessian approximations, while a dual variable enforces a measured-latency budget via per-layer LUTs. The second-order sensitivity yields group scores that allocate sparsity where curvature is low, and the dual controller continuously rebalances masks to hit a user target without post-hoc search. For N:M sparsity, each M-block is treated as a group and the proximal step reduces to second-order top-k within blocks with straight-through discretization. This unifies the post-training accuracy of OBS with the hardware guarantees of LUT-based pruning and the training-time stability of dual-controlled threshold learning.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of reducing labeling cost for training graph neural networks by designing an active learning strategy that selects which nodes to query for labels. Its key insight is to frame active node selection as a sequential decision-making problem and to learn a transferable selection policy by training a graph-based policy network with reinforcement learning on multiple fully labeled source graphs, so the policy can generalize to new target graphs. The method builds a GNN-based policy that observes graph structure, node features, and current label/learning states, outputs node-query decisions, and is trained via RL to maximize downstream GNN performance; experiments show the learned policy improves label efficiency both within and across domains.

result.text: The paper tackles offline reinforcement learning where standard off-policy methods fail due to extrapolation error from out-of-distribution (OOD) actions in a fixed dataset. Its key insight is that explicit policy constraints are unnecessary if one can quantify epistemic uncertainty and perform pessimistic value updates: penalizing Q-values where uncertainty is high prevents overestimation on OOD actions while still permitting generalization. result.text: The paper addresses how to make decentralized SGD both communication-efficient and fast-converging by choosing communication topologies that enable nearly-exact averaging with little per-iteration communication. The key insight is that exponential graphs—where each node links to O(log n) neighbors—and, notably, a schedule of log(n) one-peer exponential graphs (each node talks to a single neighbor per iteration) can together achieve exact or nearly-exact averaging while using much less communication than dense or fully synchronous topologies. result.text: The paper addresses the limited and uneven memory capacity of modern Hopfield networks, where retrieval dynamics can get stuck in many metastable states causing memory confusion. Its key insight is that a learnable feature map Φ can kernelize the Hopfield energy so that fixed points of retrieval align with local minima in kernel space, and that enforcing separation of stored patterns in this space yields a kernel-induced similarity that spreads local minima more uniformly. Methodologically, the authors introduce U-Hop, a two-stage retrieval procedure that first trains Φ via a separation loss LΦ to distribute local minima (Stage I) and then runs standard Hopfield energy minimization in the transformed space for retrieval (Stage II), empirically demonstrating reduced metastability and improved associative-memory and downstream performance compared to prior Hopfield models and similarity measures.

args.text: We propose Privacy-Adaptive Three-Point Compression (PA-3PC), a federated optimizer that embeds a randomized partial-sketch mask and time-varying contraction inside a three-point compressor, with parameters scheduled by a DP moments accountant. Clients keep an un-noised error-feedback residual locally while transmitting only a noised, randomly subsampled 3PC update; the sampling rate and contraction evolve over training to jointly amplify privacy and control compression bias/variance. This unifies privacy amplification via partial, randomized communication with dynamic compression, aiming for near-optimal privacy–utility–communication trade-offs predicted by sketch-based DP mean estimation, while extending prior DP+compression frameworks to convergent, evolving compressors. We outline analyses showing convergence under smooth nonconvexity with client-level DP and reduced bits at fixed privacy compared to fixed compressors, and validate on FL benchmarks.

We propose Adversarial Flatness Matching (AFM): augment fast single-step adversarial training with a term that explicitly flattens the adversarial loss by penalizing the variance of input gradients and a Hutchinson-style Hessian-trace proxy computed over random perturbations inside the ε-ball. Unlike GradAlign’s pairwise gradient alignment, AFM enforces low-curvature consistency across a small ensemble of perturbations, and we combine it with un-clipped, noise-initialized N-FGSM to avoid catastrophic overfitting at large ε while keeping overhead to a few extra gradient–vector products. By targeting the known mechanism where maximal FGSM concentrates training on sharp boundary points, AFM pushes adversarial optima toward flat local maxima that are known to generalize and transfer better; we further adaptively weight the penalty per batch using a curvature-certificate-based bound to focus on high-curvature regions. This yields PGD-level robustness with fast-AT efficiency and improved stability across ε scales.

result.text: The paper addresses the limitation of neural network-based wave functions that can only model different geometries of the same fixed set of atoms, preventing a single model from generalizing across molecules with different compositions. The key insight is to learn transferable local electronic representations via graph-based message passing that connect molecular orbitals to covalent bonds, enabling embeddings that capture local electronic structure common to multiple molecules. The authors introduce Globe, a graph-learned orbital embedding scheme, and Moon, a size-consistent molecular orbital network Ansatz that uses those embeddings to jointly solve Schrödinger equations for different molecules; empirically Moon converges about 4.5× faster to comparable or lower energies and yields additive energy scaling with system size where prior methods diverged. Together, Globe and Moon demonstrate for the first time that a single neural wave function can generalize across molecules with different atoms.

args.text: We propose Determinantal Quadrature Sampling (DQS) layers that combine continuous-kernel convolutions with principled node selection: each output location approximates an integral operator by selecting k continuous offsets drawn from a feature-dependent continuous volume sampling density, providing diverse coverage and near-optimal quadrature error. Concretely, we parameterize a low-rank feature map over the offset domain whose Gram matrix defines the VS log-det objective; offsets and weights are chosen via a differentiable top-k sampler that maximizes a soft log-det while modulating kernel bandwidth with scale for anti-aliasing. DQS subsumes learnable-spacing and deformable convolutions but avoids mode collapse in sampling, yields resolution-agnostic behavior, and extends to token mixers/attention by sampling key/query integration nodes in the continuous image plane. We expect gains at iso-FLOPs on high-resolution vision and irregularly sampled sequences, with stability and coverage guarantees inherited from VS theory.

We propose uncertainty-aware decentralized 3D Gaussian Splatting via expectation propagation (EP) on boundary "ghost Gaussians": each shard maintains a Gaussian (Laplace) posterior approximation over shared parameters (position, covariance, color/basis) from its local photometric likelihood, and asynchronously exchanges natural-parameter deltas (precision and mean-precision) over a rotating exponential-graph schedule. Incoming messages are fused by EP site updates (product/division of factors) to avoid double counting and to downweight stale information, while local SGLD updates provide moment estimates and Fisher-informed precisions that reflect photometric residuals. Compared to parameter averaging or master-centric ADMM, this yields barrier-free, uncertainty-calibrated consensus that is robust to heterogeneity and staleness and compresses well via low-rank precision updates for anisotropic Gaussians. Combined with Grendel-style sparse routing to only communicate factors for Gaussians influencing remote pixels, this achieves higher quality per bit and faster wall-clock convergence on large scenes.

result.text: This paper addresses the problem of certifying robustness of offline reinforcement learning against training-time poisoning attacks, where an adversary can arbitrarily manipulate a subset of training trajectories. The key insight is that by defining tractable certification criteria tailored to RL—per-state action stability and cumulative reward bounds—and by using aggregation and partitioning protocols over trajectories, one can provably bound how many poisoned trajectories a learned policy can tolerate. The authors introduce COPA, a certification framework that computes these bounds, proposes temporal and other aggregation schemes to improve robustness, and analyzes the computational limits (showing some certification variants are tight while others are NP-complete). Empirical results across algorithms and environments show the proposed aggregation methods substantially boost certified robustness and that certification tightness and tolerable poisoning vary by algorithm and environment.
